extracted.intended_audience: NLP researchers and practitioners working on patent analysis, plus patent offices and ML engineers interested in patent-focused models
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluation criteria for developing, evaluating, and deploying NLP and multimodal methods tailored to patent documents, including data, metrics, modeling, and application-specific considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of curated patent datasets
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of publicly accessible datasets for some tasks is limited; patent offices might consider providing more of their internal pre-processed databases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curated datasets specifically designed for different patent tasks are needed because offices often only offer raw PDF documents and manual reading of individual documents. Providing pre-processed, well-structured data would stimulate method development and reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benchmarks: labeled datasets and established metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Benchmarks should consist of labeled datasets and established metrics for performance evaluation, such as accuracy and precision, to enable fair and transparent comparison of methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many patent tasks rely on closed-source datasets, limiting replication. Well-defined benchmarks must be open and appropriate for the patent domain because general text evaluation metrics may not be suitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent-specific evaluation metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation metrics for patent texts are required because previous general-purpose metrics may not be appropriate for the particular language requirements of patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper notes inclusion of common text evaluation methods in an appendix but emphasizes an important research need for novel metrics that reflect legal/technical precision, clarity, and other patent-specific criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate conception of novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Research notions of 'novelty' often deviate from the strict definition in patent law; evaluations should distinguish legal novelty from metrics of oddness, perceived originality, or creativity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious when designing novelty-prediction tasks: some studies generate metrics for oddness or perceived originality rather than detecting legal novelty, which can misrepresent the task and its applicability to patent law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and evaluation of large language models (LLMs)
rubrics_metrics.description: LLMs are promising for patent analysis and generation tasks but have been under-evaluated specifically on patent-related tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because patents feature formal language, dense technical content, and legal implications, LLMs could identify nuanced patterns for classification, novelty prediction, and assist in drafting claims or descriptions. Rigorous evaluation on patent-specific tasks is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision and legal formality in generated patent text
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent documents require a specific style: formal, unambiguous language and precise, accurate, and clear descriptions and claims to satisfy legal requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of precision/range/clarity hampers examination, risks a small scope, and may provide leverage for litigation. Generation systems must aim for legal adequacy, not just naturalness or fluency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-sequence modeling to include patent descriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Many patent analysis tasks ignore long descriptions because descriptions far exceed the context length of many transformer models; integrating descriptions may significantly improve performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long-range dependencies and context retention are challenging; research should investigate long-sequence modeling approaches (and leverage LLMs with extended context windows, e.g., >100k tokens) to unlock patent-description information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multimodal methods combining text, images, and metadata
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent documents and their context include drawings and citations; multimodal models can combine multiple data types to improve patent analysis performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt architectures like CLIP or Vision Transformers to bridge textual descriptions and visual data. Applications include patent classification, image retrieval, drafting from design figures (ensuring alignment), and creating informative visualizations of patent landscapes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer sentence/paragraph embeddings over word embeddings
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentence/paragraph embeddings are preferable because they capture more nuanced contextual information from entire sentences or paragraphs than word embeddings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sentence-level or paragraph-level embeddings for tasks requiring richer contextual understanding rather than relying solely on word embeddings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model class selection: transformer-based models favored
rubrics_metrics.description: Transformer-based models (e.g., BERT, GPT) have revolutionized patent NLP and often outperform traditional machine-learning models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While deep learning and transformer methods are generally more effective, resource-limited settings may still use convolutional/recurrent networks, SVMs, or random forests. Consider computational cost vs. performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hybrid methods leveraging multiple patent sources
rubrics_metrics.description: A promising direction is to hybridize methods so they can use multiple sources from patents, including texts, images, and metadata.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combining heterogeneous inputs can improve downstream tasks (classification, retrieval, valuation) and enable richer representations of patent documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information extraction as a foundational step
rubrics_metrics.description: Information extraction serves as a primer to support various patent-related applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State-of-the-art language models can help in precise extraction of entities/relations to improve performance in downstream applications such as classification, landscaping, and similarity measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address data quality and accessibility issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Current publication modes (PDFs, poor scans, rudimentary classification) and restrictions on automated processing hinder training and analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent offices should provide better access, structured registries, and pre-processed datasets to enable large-scale automated processing. Fixing extraction quality and providing machine-readable formats is critical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on under-investigated application areas
rubrics_metrics.description: Tasks such as grant prediction, litigation prediction, patent valuation, and automated formal novelty/inventiveness detection are comparatively less investigated and deserve more attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research should expand beyond routine tasks (classification/retrieval) to support patent examination workflows (formal novelty detection, inventiveness), legal argument derivation, and motions support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propose open-sourced datasets and benchmarks for new tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: When proposing novel patent tasks, authors should suggest open-sourced datasets and benchmarks for future research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open datasets and benchmarks promote reproducibility and fair comparison; avoid reliance on closed-source corpora.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of computational costs for large-scale patent corpora
rubrics_metrics.description: Large language models would impose overwhelming computational burdens if required to process very large bodies of patent text; some patent tasks depend more on problem definition and mapping to pattern-identification than sheer model size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design problems to leverage conventional pattern-identification and statistics where appropriate; balance model complexity with tractability for large-scale patent analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multimodal approaches to support drafting and alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Multimodal models can assist in patent drafting from design figures and ensure textual descriptions and figures are aligned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply multimodal architectures to generate or refine descriptions that correspond accurately to figures, improving clarity and reducing inconsistency between drawings and text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge domain-specific language complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent texts are highly artificial: precise language combined with technical complexity creates a specialized language that requires specific training and experience to read and interpret.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systems and evaluations should account for atypical vocabulary and formulations that deviate from everyday language or even domain-expert vocabulary; models may need domain adaptation and specialized pretraining.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage retrieval and similarity methods for prior art search
rubrics_metrics.description: Automated search for prior art benefits from full-text similarity search and retrieval-oriented metrics and campaigns (e.g., CLEF-IP, TREC-like evaluations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use retrieval benchmarks and metrics oriented to recall and precision in patent retrieval tasks; enrich embeddings with global context to improve retrieval effectiveness.
